Why must font measurement match the drawn face?

Both rows draw “Ink on paper” in EB Garamond. Each marker adds the same 0.5-unit gap, but the upper row placed it using JetBrains Mono’s 6.48-unit measurement rather than Garamond’s 4.41. That puts it 2.07 units too far right. Where does the phrase’s width come from?

Transcript

Diagram widths: Measured in EB Garamond

  1. Measure the wrong face and the marker lands 2.07 units too far

    Same phrase, size and 0.5-unit gap; only the measurement changes.

    Both rows draw “Ink on paper” in EB Garamond. Each marker adds the same 0.5-unit gap, but the upper row placed it using JetBrains Mono’s 6.48-unit measurement rather than Garamond’s 4.41. That puts it 2.07 units too far right. Where does the phrase’s width come from?

    • Ink on paper. Measured as Mono: 6.48. Ink on paper. Measured as Garamond: 4.41.
  2. A phrase’s width is the sum of its glyphs’ advances

    Ticks: where each glyph hands the pen to the next. Dashed: the 2 spaces.

    Each glyph moves the pen on by its advance, and the next glyph starts where the pen stopped. The dashed cells are spaces, which move the pen without drawing anything. The ruler adds up all 12 advances, which is how the lower row placed its marker. Measure the face you draw: each face and cut gives the same text its own advances.

    • A dimension line marked “4.41 units”;
    • A tick under “Ink on paper” at each of its 11 pen positions, and dashed cells around its 2 spaces.
  3. The upper marker went 0.5 past a JetBrains Mono ruler

    Upper ticks: Garamond’s advances, as drawn. Lower: JetBrains Mono’s, as measured.

    This is the opening’s upper row, with both measurements laid under the words from the same start. Each slanted line joins a Garamond pen stop to the same stop in JetBrains Mono. Every Garamond glyph here advances less than Mono’s 0.54, so the lines lean further apart at each glyph and the rulers end 2.07 units apart. The filled marker sits 0.5 past the Mono ruler’s end, as the layout placed it. The ring sits 0.5 past the Garamond ruler’s end, where the lower row put its marker.

    • “Ink on paper” in Garamond, as in the opening’s upper row, with its filled marker 6.98 units from the start. Under it, two rulers from the same start: Garamond’s 12 advances, ending at 4.41, and JetBrains Mono’s, ending at 6.48; thin lines join matching pen stops and spread apart glyph by glyph. A filled marker 0.5 past the Mono ruler’s end, a ring 0.5 past Garamond’s.
  4. Bold and italic are faces of their own, with their own advances

    Same text, size 0.9: three cuts, three widths.

    Regular, Bold and Italic supply different glyphs and metrics. Bold here advances farther than Regular, so a marker placed using Regular’s measurement would leave less room after the bold words. The cut must agree between measurement and drawing, just as the font family must.

    • The same words in three EB Garamond cuts: Regular, advance 4.41; Bold, advance 4.85; Italic, advance 4.24. Each cut was requested and captured from its own source font.
  5. Measured in EB Garamond first, each box fits its word

    Under each box: how far its word was stretched to fit. Here, not at all.

    Rayner measures Ink and Paper in EB Garamond before the layout sizes their boxes. Both words keep their natural proportions, so both stretch factors are ×1.000. If the layout had used Inter’s estimates instead, would both words stretch by the same factor?

    • Flowchart: 2 nodes, 1 link:
      • “stretched ×1.000” beside Ink (note);
      • “stretched ×1.000” beside Paper (note);
      • Ink;
      • Ink → Paper;
      • Paper.

    Same text, size 0.9: three cuts, three widths.

    Regular, Bold and Italic supply different glyphs and metrics. Bold here advances farther than Regular, so a marker placed using Regular’s measurement would leave less room after the bold words. The cut must agree between measurement and drawing, just as the font family must.

  5. Laid out from Inter estimates, the Garamond words are stretched

    Under each box: how far its word was stretched to fit the width Inter would need.

    The layout used Inter estimates, then the renderer fitted the Garamond words to those recorded widths. Each factor is a word’s recorded width over its own Garamond advance, and Paper’s is larger than Ink’s, so no single scale turns Inter widths into Garamond ones. This is the misplaced marker’s problem again: one face was measured and another drawn.

    • Flowchart: 2 nodes, 1 link:
      • “stretched ×1.135” beside Ink (note);
      • “stretched ×1.399” beside Paper (note);
      • Ink;
      • Ink → Paper;
      • Paper.

Check yourself

  1. Reverse the opening’s mistake: measure “Ink on paper” in EB Garamond, draw it in JetBrains Mono, and put the marker 0.5 units after the measured width. Where does the marker land?

    Show the answer

    On the words. It goes 4.41 + 0.5 = 4.91 units from the start, but the JetBrains Mono phrase runs to 6.48, so the marker sits about 1.57 units before the phrase ends.

  2. A layout measures the phrase in Regular and puts a marker 0.5 units after it, but the phrase is drawn in Bold. What happens to the gap?

    Show the answer

    It shrinks from 0.5 to 0.06 units: Bold advances 0.44 further than Regular at size 0.9, so the marker nearly touches the words.

  3. Add a trailing space, “Ink on paper ”. No ink changes. Does the marker move?

    Show the answer

    Yes. The space has an advance, so the measured width grows by that advance, and the marker, placed after the width, moves right by the same amount.

  4. In some other diagram, a box reads “stretched ×1.000”. What does that say about how its word was measured?

    Show the answer

    Its recorded width equals the drawn word’s own advance: the layout measured the face, cut and size the renderer drew, or a face that happens to give that word the same advance.
